```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      eval = torch::torch_is_installed())
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)
r_vec <- function(t) as.numeric(as.array(t))
```

A graph neural network layer updates each node from messages sent along its
incoming edges. For node $i$ with incoming neighbors $\mathcal{N}(i)$,

$$
h_i' = \gamma\left(h_i,\ \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \phi(h_i, h_j, e_{ji})\right),
$$

where $\phi$ builds a message, $\bigoplus$ is a permutation invariant
aggregation such as sum, mean, or max, and $\gamma$ updates the node. This
article shows the pieces graphlearnR uses to compute this and how the built in
layers fit the pattern.

## Scatter aggregation

Aggregation is a *scatter*: row $k$ of a message matrix is added (or
averaged, or maximized) into row `index[k]` of the output. Rows that receive
nothing are zero.

```{r}
msg <- torch_tensor(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), ncol = 1))
index <- c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 4L)
cbind(sum = r_vec(scatter_sum(msg, index, 4)),
      mean = r_vec(scatter_mean(msg, index, 4)),
      max = r_vec(scatter_max(msg, index, 4)),
      count = r_vec(scatter_count(index, 4)))
```

Node 3 receives no messages, so every aggregation returns 0 for it rather
than a missing value or negative infinity. `scatter_softmax()` normalizes
scores within each group, which attention layers use.

```{r}
r_vec(scatter_softmax(msg, index, 4))
```

All of these are vectorized torch operations, so they run on the GPU and are
differentiable.

## The general operator

`message_passing()` implements the equation above. By default the message is
the source features, optionally scaled by `edge_weight`.

```{r}
x <- torch_tensor(matrix(c(1, 10, 100), ncol = 1))
ei <- torch_tensor(rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(3, 3, 1)), dtype = torch_long())
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, aggr = "sum"))
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, aggr = "mean"))
```

Node 3 receives from nodes 1 and 2, node 1 from node 3, and node 2 from no
one.

A custom message function is called with named arguments `x_j` (source
features), `x_i` (target features), `edge_attr`, `edge_weight`, `index` (the
target of each edge), and `num_nodes`, one row per edge. Accept the ones you
need and `...` for the rest. Here is a message that is the
difference between source and target, the core of EdgeConv:

```{r}
diff_msg <- function(x_j, x_i, ...) x_j - x_i
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, message = diff_msg, aggr = "max"))
```

## Writing a layer

A layer is a torch `nn_module` whose `forward()` calls `message_passing()`.
This one implements a mean aggregator with separate weights for the node and
its neighbors:

```{r}
my_conv <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(in_features, out_features) {
    self$lin_self <- nn_linear(in_features, out_features)
    self$lin_nbr <- nn_linear(in_features, out_features, bias = FALSE)
  },
  forward = function(x, edge_index) {
    agg <- message_passing(x, edge_index, aggr = "mean")
    self$lin_self(x) + self$lin_nbr(agg)
  }
)

g <- dataset_karate()
tt <- graph_tensors(g)
torch_manual_seed(1)
layer <- my_conv(34, 4)
dim(layer(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
```

That is the GraphSAGE update, which graphlearnR also provides as
`sage_conv()`.

## Built in layers

| layer | update | edge input |
|---|---|---|
| `sage_conv()` | $W_1 h_i + W_2 \operatorname{mean}_{j} h_j$ | none |
| `gcn_conv()` | $\sum_j \frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat d_i \hat d_j}} W h_j$ with self loops | weights |
| `graph_conv()` | $W_1 h_i + W_2 \sum_j w_{ji} h_j$ | weights |
| `gin_conv()` | $\operatorname{MLP}((1 + \epsilon) h_i + \sum_j h_j)$ | optional features (GINE) |
| `gat_conv()` | attention weighted sum, multiple heads | optional features |
| `gatv2_conv()` | GATv2 dynamic attention | optional features |
| `transformer_conv()` | scaled dot product attention over neighbors | optional features |
| `nn_conv()` | $W_1 h_i + \sum_j \Theta(e_{ji}) h_j$ (edge conditioned) | features, required |
| `rgcn_conv()` | $W_0 h_i + \sum_r \operatorname{mean}_{j \in \mathcal{N}_r(i)} W_r h_j$ | relation type, required |

Every layer takes `(x, edge_index, ...)` and returns new node features.

```{r}
torch_manual_seed(2)
layers <- list(
  sage = sage_conv(34, 8),
  gcn = gcn_conv(34, 8),
  gin = gin_conv(graph_mlp(c(34, 16, 8))),
  gat = gat_conv(34, 4, heads = 2),
  transformer = transformer_conv(34, 4, heads = 2)
)
sapply(layers, function(l) dim(l(tt$x, tt$edge_index)))
```

Attention layers keep the coefficients of their last forward pass. Within
each target node they sum to one.

```{r}
gat <- layers$gat
invisible(gat(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
alpha <- as.array(gat$last_attention$alpha)
dst <- as.array(gat$last_attention$edge_index)[2, ]
head(rowsum(alpha, dst))
```

### Bipartite input

Most layers also accept a pair `list(x_src, x_dst)` when sources and targets
are different node sets with different feature sizes. Give the input size as
a pair too. Heterogeneous models are built on this.

```{r}
xs <- torch_randn(5, 3)
xd <- torch_randn(2, 7)
bip <- torch_tensor(rbind(c(1, 2, 5), c(1, 2, 2)), dtype = torch_long())
dim(sage_conv(c(3, 7), 4)(list(xs, xd), bip))
```

### Edge features and relations

```{r}
torch_manual_seed(3)
ge <- dataset_karate()
ge$edge_attr <- matrix(runif(num_edges(ge) * 2), ncol = 2)
ge$edge_type <- sample(1:3, num_edges(ge), replace = TRUE)
te <- graph_tensors(ge)
dim(nn_conv(34, 8, edge_dim = 2)(te$x, te$edge_index, edge_attr = te$edge_attr))
dim(rgcn_conv(34, 8, num_relations = 3, num_bases = 2)(te$x, te$edge_index,
                                                     edge_type = te$edge_type))
```

## How the layers are tested

The test suite checks every layer for properties that must hold whatever
the weights are:

* **Permutation equivariance.** Relabeling the nodes relabels the output in
  the same way.
* **Agreement with a reference formula.** GCN is compared with the dense
  $\hat D^{-1/2} \hat A \hat D^{-1/2} X W$, GraphSAGE and GIN with explicit
  neighbor loops, and RGCN with per relation means.
* **Gradients.** Input gradients match central finite differences in double
  precision, and parameter gradients of GCN match the analytic formula.

Here is the equivariance check for GraphSAGE:

```{r}
torch_manual_seed(4)
layer <- sage_conv(34, 4)
perm <- sample.int(34)
inv <- order(perm)
gp <- g
gp$x <- g$x[perm, ]
gp$edge_index <- matrix(inv[g$edge_index], nrow = 2)
out <- as.array(layer(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
out_p <- as.array(layer(graph_tensors(gp)$x, graph_tensors(gp)$edge_index))
max(abs(out_p - out[perm, ]))
```

## Pooling

Graph level models reduce node features to one vector per graph.
`global_add_pool()`, `global_mean_pool()`, and `global_max_pool()` take the
`batch` vector; `global_attention_pool()` learns a gate; `topk_pool()` keeps
the highest scoring fraction of nodes in each graph.

```{r}
b <- graph_batch(dataset_synthetic_graphs(4, seed = 1))
tb <- graph_tensors(b)
as.array(global_mean_pool(tb$x, b$batch))
```
